Le Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel craint: The Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel fears it may have to close its doors.
Mohamed Mimoun et Abdellah Azzouz du For: Mohamed Mimoun and Abdellah Azzouz of the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel. Photo: Édouard Desroches
Bonjour, c’est Loubna avec Aya, Firas, S: Hello, it’s Loubna with Aya, Firas, Sabrina, Cindy and Aude from École Converse!
Cette semaine, nous avons appris que le: This week, we learned that the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel was in danger. To understand the consequences of a possible closure, we spent an evening with the community organization’s team and about ten of the young people who are regulars at its space.
Autour d’un repas pas très diététique, m: Over a meal that wasn’t exactly healthy, but was comforting, we listened to their concerns to understand why they are facing such serious financial difficulties and why it is so important that the organization continue to exist.
<strong>Baisse des subventions publiques: Cuts to public funding, a rise in requests for support, structural difficulties: the community sector is struggling. The Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel is no exception and fears it may have to close its doors. In the heart of a neighbourhood facing major social challenges, including youth violence, the Forum Jeunesse has reached an impasse, and the lack of stable funding could sound the death knell for an organization that has served young people and their families for more than 20 years. Our report.
Des canapés marron vieillis par tous les: Brown couches worn down by all the teenagers who have sat on them, a pool table in the middle of the room where games are played every day, bookshelves groaning under the weight of books, a basic kitchen to stave off hunger and a few computers at the back. The Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel is a big open space where the doors are always open, and where listening and support are at the heart of the work. But today, the mood is gloomy and the atmosphere downcast. The organization, like so many others in the community sector, has run out of funding and doesn’t know how to carry on its mission.
« Si ça ferme demain, je ne sais pas ce: “If it closes tomorrow, I don’t know what I’ll do,” says one of the young people who come here. Over a hamburger and a few fries, about ten of them have agreed to open up to La Converse. “The Forum is my family, it’s the only place we can go to hang out with friends, to get help if we have a problem, to take part in activities…” confirms Samy from behind his blue-tinted sunglasses.
Dans le quartier de Saint-Michel, le For: In the Saint-Michel neighbourhood, the Forum Jeunesse is much more than a community centre: it’s a refuge, a springboard, a space of hope for many young people looking for direction. Every young person who walks through the door has a broad smile, a sincere joy at being back. Here, everyone knows everyone, and nobody judges anybody. Everyone arrives with baggage that is more or less heavy, with experiences that are more or less painful, and sets it down here. More than just a space, the Forum is a place where young people like Samy find support, guidance and a chance to rebuild their future.
Sa fermeture signifierait la perte d’un: Its closure would mean the loss of an essential service in a neighbourhood that badly needs it. A possibility that deeply worries Samy and the other young people. “I can’t imagine what it would be like if the Forum closes… The people here aren’t just friends, they’re my second family. During the holidays, I already had a hard time not coming, so if it closes, a lot of young people will go back to the street, that’s for sure,” says the 19-year-old.
Car le Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel es: Because the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel is first and foremost a place that offers these young people activities, an alternative to the street, the only other place where they can hang out with friends, but where they become targets for recruiters from criminal networks. “What I like best about the Forum is that we do activities all together, like on Saturdays, when we cook for people experiencing homelessness and go hand out the meals at Berri-UQAM. I like it because we’re helping others,” says Soulim.
Soccer, rédaction de CV, simulations d’e: Soccer, résumé writing, mock job interviews, awareness-raising, games, community radio, making video clips to denounce street harassment, meetings with prisoners: the projects run with the young people are as varied as they are useful. “Everything we do is a way of doing social intervention, showing them another path, letting them reveal who they are,” explains Abdellah Azzouz, the only youth worker on staff, who hasn’t been paid for two weeks. Because the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel is at risk for one reason only: money.
Avant l’arrivée de Mohamed Mimoun au loc: Before Mohamed Mimoun arrives at the space that evening, the young people can’t stop praising the Forum’s coordinator. “He’s someone who has devoted himself to the organization for more than 15 years, who doesn’t count his hours, who answers worried parents at 2 a.m., who never says no when we need him, even on weekends! But he’s still a human being, and we worry about him, because he can’t keep doing everything like this. The Forum Jeunesse doesn’t exist because of its space, it exists because of Momo,” sums up Adam, the chair of the organization’s board of directors.
En effet, Mohamed Mimoun n’est pas du ge: Indeed, Mohamed Mimoun is not the type to complain all day long. A husband and the father of a child with autism, he devotes all his time to the young people. One of the main difficulties facing the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel lies in the management of its funding, which is often insufficient and one-off.
« Le problème, c’est que les subventions: “The problem is that grants are awarded project by project and for one year only. There is no funding to pay for the actual operation of the organization, starting with the $3,000 monthly rent for this space,” explains the man everyone affectionately calls Momo. “We were already lucky to find a landlord who agreed to rent to an organization that works with young people, because landlords often don’t want to. But we’ve only been here for two years. After working as a roving organization for years, we finally have a place that has become a hangout for these young people, but we’re already at risk of losing it, because we couldn’t pay the rent this month.”
Ce système de financement par projet, où: This project-based funding system, in which every initiative depends on time-limited grants, leaves the organization in a precarious position. Although special funding was awarded to it last year to fight violence, “it wasn’t renewed,” laments Momo, who was counting on that money to continue his activities. He can’t hold back his tears as he talks about the situation.
Dans son dernier budget, l’arrondissemen: In its latest budget, the borough of Villeray–Saint-Michel–Parc-Extension does not, in fact, provide any grant to the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel. Yet other organizations, whose role is important but which are not specialized in violence prevention, do receive funding, youth workers lament.
Sollicitée pour une entrevue, la mairess: When we requested an interview, the borough mayor, Laurence Lavigne Lalonde, was “not available.” Her communications department did, however, send us the following message: “The Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel offers important activities for young people in our borough. The City supports them financially through provincial funding, and at the borough level, we support them by, among other things, providing them with a space. We’re doing our part, we’re going to keep doing it, and we hope the organization will manage to balance its budget as it has in previous years.” When she refers to a space provided to the organization, the mayor is talking about an administrative office in the basement of the library, which was indeed allocated to the organization by previous municipal authorities. It is not the space that welcomes the young people.
« Nous en avons assez de travailler sur: “We’re fed up with working on one-off projects. It’s essential to be able to offer projects that are funded over several years,” says Mohamed Mimoun, like many other community players. This uncertainty about the future of the Forum Jeunesse’s funding threatens not only the continuity of its activities, but also the organization’s ability to meet the growing needs of young people and their parents.
En plus des jeunes, des parents désespér: In addition to the young people, desperate parents knock on the Forum’s door every day, looking for a listening ear and solutions to increasingly tense family situations.
« Mon téléphone sonne constamment, et pl: “My phone rings constantly, and more and more often it’s about radicalization prevention; these are calls from parents,” says Mohamed Mimoun. The intensity in his voice betrays the weight of the work. “We have been directly affected by violence, because we’ve lost young people in our neighbourhood. It affected the Maghrebi community a great deal.” The organization, which has built a reputation for expertise in crisis management and youth violence, steps into crisis situations by providing mediation to families. The calls Mohamed Mimoun receives thus come from anguished parents, often at a loss when a child has disappeared or is involved in delinquent acts.
Malgré la surcharge de travail, le manqu: Despite the overload of work and the lack of funding and staff, the organization continues to offer support to young people and their families. “When I get a call from a mother in tears, even if I’m not getting paid and even if it’s 11 p.m., I can’t say no,” explains Momo. “Recently, a young guy told me he’d been offered $500 to smash up a car. If I’m not there to answer him and remind him why he shouldn’t do it, he might be tempted.”
Avec autant de demandes, le travail labo: With so many requests, the laborious work of searching for funding often takes a back seat. “We have a small team on the ground that knows its community well, but it’s a community that remains marginalized and not sufficiently organized,” points out Mohamed Mimoun.
Cette absence de structuration et de rés: This lack of structure and of a solid support network in the community sector makes the organization even more vulnerable to funding crises. Today, it has no choice but to call for help. “We’re looking for funders who would want to fund our mission. If we could at least cover the $36,000 in annual rent, it would give us room to breathe. After that, we’ll see…” says the youth worker.
Il est épuisé, mais il entend mener le c: He is exhausted, but he intends to fight to the end for the young people who count on him and for the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel team. Ready to contribute to this fight, several of these young people shared their stories with us and explained how meeting the organization was a turning point for them. Here are their stories.
Originaire d’Algérie, Samy pense passer: Originally from Algeria, Samy thought he was going to spend a vacation at his father’s when he arrived in Canada at 15. “They hid the truth from me because they knew I would refuse to leave and to leave behind my grandparents, the ones who raised me,” he says with a sigh. Having left without saying goodbye, he suffered a shock so strong that he withdrew into himself for months, refused to adapt to his new reality and sank into depression.
« Je passais tout mon temps dans ma cham: “I spent all my time in my room, shut in, without talking to anyone. Until the day I cracked and wanted to hurt myself,” the young man says with restraint. When he understood that he wouldn’t be going back to his home country, he began to accept the idea of going to school, but fell in with the wrong crowd. “I made mistakes, I followed people who led me down the wrong road. I did stupid stuff, I tried things…” he admits. But it was in making those mistakes that something clicked. “The day I narrowly escaped serious trouble with the law, I understood that I wanted something else for myself. I changed who I hung out with, and that’s when I discovered the Forum Jeunesse. It changed everything, it really helped me get out of it.”
C’est grâce à un ami qu’il commence à fr: It was thanks to a friend that he began coming to this community space, at first timidly, then more regularly. “I met Momo and Abdellah Azzouz. They did everything for me, no matter what my problems were: family, money, even with the law. Here, I found people who listen to me, who understand me and who really help me. Momo is a father to me, I spend more time with him than with my own father, and Azzouz is like a brother.”
Aujourd’hui, Samy est déterminé à aller: Today, Samy is determined to move forward, despite the tension that still exists with his family and the fact that he has no place to live. He is looking for a job, trying to lead a more stable life and has found his path. “Azzouz inspires me enormously. I’d like to be the next generation of Azzouz’s work. I’d like to help people the way I was helped,” he says.
<strong>Ramzi, 17 ans : « Momo, c’est co: Ramzi, 17: “Momo is like my second father, and Azzouz is like my big brother”
« Si le Forum ne nous guidait pas dans l: “If the Forum wasn’t guiding us in the right direction, we wouldn’t like this Forum.” Ramzi, who is 17, says these words with a smile. The young man comes straight from the lively corners of Masson Street. He ended up at the Forum Jeunesse a little over three months ago. It was during a game of “foot,” as he calls it, that his “guy Ayoub” told him about the Forum and invited him to meet Momo and Azzouz. This space full of colour, books, cozy corners, activities and photos has become an oasis for the young man, who enjoys the encounters, the atmosphere and the friends he makes there.
À son jeune âge, il a fait le choix d’ar: At a young age, he chose to stop going to school and wanted to enter the working world very quickly. Having arrived in Montréal in 2019, he found himself in a reception class and didn’t particularly enjoy the experience. So he preferred to interrupt his studies, despite his good grades, and devote all his energy to looking for a job in the field he’s passionate about: boxing. It was at the Forum that he found the support he needed to carry out his plans.
Momo lui a été d’une aide immense dans s: Momo was an immense help in his job search, he explains. He showed him how to write his résumé and guided him to a boxing gym. Momo also spoke with a boxing coach, and the teenager hopes to start training very soon.
En plus d’être une source d’encouragemen: As well as being a source of encouragement and support, the Forum is also a second family for Ramzi. “Momo is like my second father, and Azzouz is like my big brother, and I have friends here who are like my brothers – I love them all,” he says, visibly happy. At the Forum, he plays soccer, cooks and goes on outings in good company that keep him on the right path. For him, if the Forum were to close, “it wouldn’t be good for [us].” Many young people would find themselves with nothing to do, he laments. “If they don’t come to the Forum, some young people will go in the wrong direction.”
<strong>Bouchra, 28 ans : du Forum Jeune: Bouchra, 28: from the Forum Jeunesse to a master’s in sociology
À 28 ans, Bouchra porte en elle l’emprei: At 28, Bouchra carries the indelible mark of the Forum Jeunesse. Eight years ago, while still a CEGEP student, she pushed open the door of this space buzzing with exchange and reflection. Today, although her life has taken her elsewhere, the bond she maintains with the Forum and with Momo, her pillar, remains intact. “For me, the Forum is like a home. When I go to Algeria, I visit my family. Here, it’s the same. It’s a space that has always welcomed me in difficult times.”
Elle habite à proximité et y passe régul: She lives nearby and drops in regularly, just to say hello, catch up, soak up this familiar atmosphere where she learned so much. For her, the Forum was more than a meeting place: “It was a school of social, community and political engagement, and of reflection. The Forum plants seeds, but you don’t realize it when you’re young and you’re going there. It’s much later that you realize the effect it had on you.”
En replongeant dans ses souvenirs, son r: As she dives back into her memories, her eyes light up. She sees again those Friday evenings when, surrounded by other young people her age, she debated burning current affairs issues. “At the time, we were in the middle of the debate on the Charter of Values, Islamophobia and this whole social context in turmoil.” The discussions were passionate, the questions many and, above all, the sense of belonging was unshakable.
Le Forum lui a ouvert des horizons insou: The Forum opened up unsuspected horizons for her. Guests came to share their expertise: master’s students, researchers, politicians… A fascinating world, to which she would probably not have had access otherwise. “Momo pushed us to get involved. He would say, ‘Here, next week, you’re the one who’s presenting.’ And it took you out of your comfort zone. In the moment, you wondered why he was putting you in those situations, but he knew what he was doing.”
Tout l’art de Momo est là : voir en chaq: That is the whole art of Momo: seeing in every young person a potential that they themselves don’t yet dare to recognize. “He has this ability to see in us what we can’t see yet. He pushes us, he guides us, but without hurting us. He accompanies us.”
Aujourd’hui, Bouchra est étudiante à la: Today, Bouchra is a master’s student in sociology at UQAM. Her thesis project is about loneliness and isolation among Maghrebi men in Quebec, a theme that resonates deeply with her own journey. Of Algerian origin, she arrived in Quebec at 16, with a vague feeling that she didn’t have the legitimacy to take a position on Quebec’s social issues.
« Mais en m’engageant au Forum, j’ai déc: “But by getting involved at the Forum, I discovered my interest in social issues. My first student jobs were in the community sector. I worked for Bon Resto Saint-Michel, a very important food security organization in the neighbourhood. Then, at university, I joined associations, including a group that sponsors refugee students. Even today, no matter where I am, I feel concerned about society.”
Avec une assurance tranquille, le jeune: With quiet confidence, the 18-year-old guides us through the space. His purple-tinted sunglasses and his cap complete his laid-back look. A half-smile shows us how attached he is to this place. “It’s good for young people,” he says, thinking back on everything the Forum has given him since he arrived in Montréal.
Originaire d’Algérie, Mahmoud débarque d: Originally from Algeria, Mahmoud landed in the city alone, for a vacation in March 2023. A few months later, friends introduced him to the Forum, a place that quickly became an anchor for him. After a brief return to Algeria, he came back to Montréal six months ago to settle here.
Mahmoud est coiffeur et passionné de soc: Mahmoud is a barber and is passionate about soccer. In fact, he has just come back from practice when we meet him at the Forum. He lives in Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve and goes to the Forum regularly. There, he sees his friends, has a good time with them, tells them about his latest adventures. You often find him with a pool cue in his hand, waiting for his turn, ready to cash in the points. But the Forum isn’t just a place to meet and have fun for him. Every Tuesday, after his training at the Stade de Montréal, he stops by. It’s like a ritual. On Saturdays, he swaps his soccer ball for cooking utensils and takes part in the cooking workshops, another activity he particularly enjoys.
« Le vendredi, il y a de belles soirées: “On Fridays, there are great evenings,” he says proudly, a sparkle in his eyes. “Sometimes singers come. There are also activities with firefighters and police officers,” he adds. He pictures himself in those roles, with everything he is learning.
Comme beaucoup d’autres jeunes qui fréqu: Like many other young people who come to the Forum, he considers Mohamed Mimoun, a.k.a. Momo, a second father, the one he can talk to about things he couldn’t confide to anyone else. Every time Momo comes up, he smiles and his face lights up, a gleam of respect and admiration in his eyes.
Pour Mahmoud, le rôle de Momo est struct: For Mahmoud, Momo’s role is a steadying one. He helps him discover himself, build himself up and find opportunities. Mahmoud is even considering leaving hairdressing to devote himself entirely to a football career, after signing a contract with a team. Although he has played the sport since childhood, the time he puts into it while also coming to the Forum has pushed him toward new professional horizons, he says.
Alors, lorsque sa sœur est venue lui ren: So when his sister came to visit, it was only natural that he brought her to the Forum: for him, it is essential to show his family what he considers his second source of support. Although he very much wants to return to Algeria to visit his mother and loved ones, Mahmoud is proud of the life he has built here in Montréal. He even cuts the hair of Forum members, including Momo’s son – a way of giving back that reflects his community spirit.
Islem, 17 ans, est arrivé à Montréal cet: Islem, 17, arrived in Montréal this summer from Kabylia, in northeastern Algeria, with his family. He dropped his bag at his welcome class, and his cleats at Henri-Bourassa. It was on the field that he heard about the Forum and Azzouz. His friends, who go there to relax and trash-talk after games, told him about it. Very quickly, he felt at home there, in a true “second home.”
Au sein de ce qui est devenu sa « deuxiè: Within what has become his “second family,” Islem doesn’t sit idle. On Saturday mornings, he has his hands full. “We learn teamwork and sharing, and I’m passionate about it,” he says. At the Forum, the youth prepare meals for people experiencing homelessness downtown. At 9 a.m., he arrives in the Forum’s kitchen on Jarry Street, where since 2020 young people from Saint-Michel have been preparing and serving meals to the most vulnerable.
Avec sa bonne humeur, Islem coordonne l’: With his good humour, Islem coordinates the team of budding cooks. A cook for a day? Maybe not. The experience matters to him: “This activity gives me experience, and maybe one day I’ll be able to work as a kitchen helper.” On Saturday, the young Kabyle handed out meals with his friends at Berri-UQAM: “It was salad, potatoes and a piece of fruit.” For him, it is also an extra dose of altruism: “It was a special feeling, Saturday. It’s great to do good for others.”
Au sujet des difficultés financières qui: Asked about the financial difficulties threatening the centre’s survival, Islem has just one word: “Sadness!” Then he adds: “We need help – for language classes, to have games and ways to relax.” He glances at the board at the back of the room, where the schedule of activities is written in chalk.
Comme Azzouz et Momo, le grand frère et: Like Azzouz and Momo, the big brother and the father of the group, Islem has no intention of giving up. And he keeps a bright outlook: “Even if we lose the space, we’ll find solutions. Anyway, I’ll stay loyal to my group here!” Like his friends, Islem is determined to do whatever it takes to keep the Forum alive.

À 17 ans, Yuna Mohamed Amine porte en lu: At 17, Yuna Mohamed Amine carries the quiet strength of those who learn to rebuild themselves far from what they know. Originally from Algeria, he has lived in Saint-Léonard for two and a half years. And while his body travelled, his heart wandered for a long time, searching for a refuge.
L’intégration n’a pas été immédiate. Les: Fitting in was not immediate. The first months in Canada were spent in a heavy solitude, marked by hours in front of a screen playing video games, as if to fill the void. Then, one day, a friend handed him a key. “Come see, there’s a place, we hang out, we joke around together.” That simple invitation changed everything.
Cinq mois après avoir franchi les portes: Five months after walking through the Forum’s doors, Amine speaks of it with endless gratitude. Unlike his classmates at school, whom he calls “acquaintances,” here he speaks of brothers. Not just a string of faces passed in school hallways, but a brotherhood woven from laughter, challenges and closeness. With them, he shares a history, a language, a longing for home, but also a common drive toward the future.
Et, en plus de l’amitié, le Forum lui a: And besides friendship, the Forum gave him something essential: there he discovered the taste for pushing himself further. He loves the academic challenges where gift cards are at stake. “I’ve already won twice!” he says proudly. Where school imposes desks and rules, the Forum has managed to turn learning into a stimulating, almost playful challenge.
Toutefois, au-delà des jeux et des discu: Yet beyond the games and the conversations, the Forum has above all become a remedy for exile. For Amine, the most painful part of leaving his country was not adapting to a new life, but losing his grandmother without being able to say a final goodbye. Exile tore a family away from him, but the Forum gave him a new one.
Ici, il a tissé des liens profonds, fait: Here, he has forged deep bonds, made of closeness and support, a brotherhood born of uprooting, where everyone carries a story that echoes his own. Today, Amine no longer feels like a stranger. He is at home.
<strong>Soulim, 13 ans : « Il n’y a pas: Soulim, 13: “There’s no other place like the Forum”
« C’est une deuxième maison. » Voilà ce: “It’s a second home.” That is what the Forum means to young Soulim. Having lived in Montréal for a few years now, the 13-year-old lives in the heart of the vibrant Saint-Michel neighbourhood. He discovered the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel through his older brother, who spent a few months there before him. In this warm space, filled with laughter and conversation, Soulim found things to do. He likes the activities offered there, especially football and pool.
Momo et Azzouz sont des modèles qui lui: Momo and Azzouz are role models who give him good advice and teach him to avoid making mistakes. The Forum has also helped him a lot to learn French, to manage his behaviour, to better understand how the city works and to improve at school, he explains.
Pour Soulim, « il n’y a pas d’autre endr: For Soulim, “there’s no other place like the Forum.” This place is unique. The young man believes it is important for the neighbourhood’s youth that this place stay open. Tous ces récits de jeunes sont autant de: All these young people’s stories are proof of the positive impact of the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel. With their backs against the wall, the team has launched an <l1>online fundraiser</l1> and is appealing to the community for solidarity. Mohamed Mimoun also hopes that funders will be receptive to the cause of an organization that is essential to the neighbourhood’s vitality.
